title: How to Create a Line of Credit Account in QuickBooks Online (Step-By-Step) [2026 guide]
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: In today's video, I'm going to teach you how to create a line of credit account in QuickBooks Online. Having a line of credit account set up in QuickBooks is essential for tracking borrowed funds and repayments accurately within your financial records. Whether you're managing a small business or keeping personal finances in order, this process will help you stay organized and ensure your books are complete and up to date. If you don't already have a QuickBooks Online account, you can use the link in the description to sign up and get started. Now, let's dive into the steps. First, start by logging into your QuickBooks Online account and navigating to your dashboard. Look to the top right corner of the screen where you'll see a small gear icon. This is your settings menu. Go ahead and click on it to open the options. From the dropdown menu that appears, you'll need to scroll down and select the option labeled "Chart of accounts." This is where all your accounts are managed and organized within QuickBooks. Once you're on the chart of accounts page, look towards the upper right corner of the screen again and click the button labeled "New." This will allow you to create a new account. Next, you'll need to enter a name for the account you're setting up. You can choose something straightforward like "Line of Credit," or use a name that better suits your specific needs. It's helpful to pick a name that makes the account easily recognizable when you're reviewing your records later. After naming the account, it's time to assign the correct account type. In the dropdown menu for account type, select "Long-term Liabilities." This category is appropriate because a line of credit typically represents a financial obligation that spans longer than a year. Once you've set the account type, move to the detail type field. From this list, choose "Notes Payable." This detail type is the most accurate for a line of credit, as it represents loans or borrowings that need to be repaid. Finally, click the "Save" button to complete the process and create your new line of credit account. Once saved, the account will appear in your chart of accounts list, and you'll be able to use it to track transactions related to your line of credit. And that's it! You've successfully created a line of credit account in QuickBooks Online. If you found this video helpful, please like and subscribe.

title: Diary Entry I Wanted To Share With ALL Footballers...
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I wanted to share with you guys a diary entry that I wrote during a time that felt like nothing was going smoothly. And you might want to save this video for later because someday you're going to need it. Recently, I've been questioning why nothing in my life seems to be going smoothly. I've been playing football at a high level for years, training harder than everybody else, taking it more seriously than ever before. And still, I'm sitting here with no confirmed answer about where I'm playing next season. Football is competitive, I understand. I have been trying to get my European visa for the past year. I made three different applications and eventually left the country hopeless. And just two days after leaving, they called me for the acceptance meeting. Just two days after I'm out of the country, probably just bad timing, right? I graduated school with a top 1% mark, went to the best university in my country, signed with a professional club, and made a system so strong it changed the lives of 300 players remotely worldwide. And yet, parents are still skeptical to work with me and delay for months just to say no. Probably just a bad coincidence, right? This might be unrelated, but I even approached a trusted brand of dental braces, and halfway through the treatment, I was the first client in company history who had manufacturing issues, so I had to restart the process. And when they sent me the new one, the package got held at customs, and now I have no idea where the $4,000 worth of dental braces are. Just simple procedures that were initially planned to run smoothly and take a few months to complete are now becoming a headache because it's taking a few years to overcome. This is the side of football, the side of life that nobody ever talks about. Every single year without fail, I go through a season like this, a stretch where nothing seems to click, where it feels like the universe itself has turned against me. And here's the lesson I learned from this and what I wanted to share with you guys today. The toughest battles in life are given to the strongest warriors, not because life is cruel but because life is precise. The moment you decide to achieve something amazing, the moment you decide to become a professional footballer, the universe will place you in difficult situations to see what you're made of, to see whether you'll push through to the other side or whether you'll make excuses, blame the system, and quietly walk away from your dream like most people do. Most footballers quit before the breakout even happens, not because they weren't talented enough but because they stopped one season too early. And here's a harsh truth: for the majority of your life, you're going to be in the fight, you're going to be grinding, uncertain if it's going to work out, waiting for the right moment, pushing through the season when nothing feels fair. And then all of a sudden, for a small percentage of your life, everything is going to start to click. You're going to be playing your best football, your confidence is going to be untouchable, the doors are going to start opening up. And that moment right there, that moment is only beautiful because of everything that came before it. The goal in football or in life is not to avoid the hard season. The goal is to refuse to leave before the season ends. So, if you're in it right now, keep training, keep building, keep showing up every single day for your standards when everything around you feels like it's not. You will only fail the moment you decide to quit, and that's a guarantee. So, do not stop and keep pushing till the end.

title: I Called My Parents and Said "I Need Help" | Logan's Story
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Before treatment, I was I was broken. I had a lot of depression, anxiety and was using drugs and alcohol to mask all that, to cope with it. I just remember feeling so hopeless. I just broke down and I called my mom and I called my dad and I said, "I need help." I remember at that moment I I still didn't feel great but I felt for the first time that I might be headed in the right direction. In terms of choosing this treatment center, I remember there was a family friend that we had. She said, "If I had a family member going through what Logan's going through, there's only one place I would send them and that was Providence." I think walking around the center and talking to different staff, you know, a lot of the clinicians made me feel like I was understood for the first time in a in almost forever. It was also fun, too. I think that's something I didn't expect is the idea that I can work on myself and I can do the tough things and I can have the groups where I tear up and I can go into individual session and talk about things I haven't talked about but at the same time with all my peers and and even a lot of the staff I was just laughing and I was having a good time. Life now is great. I don't worry people anymore. Soon after graduating Providence, I got hired and I really just started to find my purpose and find my life. The advice I would give someone that's still struggling is stop digging. Find the people in your life who care about you and ask them for help. The answers to the questions that people might have of what happens after treatment, answer themselves when you just give into the experience. So, ask for help. Uh stop digging. I promise you that you're going to be surprised with the outcome.

title: Video 3: Why is sharing your radiotherapy treatment story important to you?
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: It's been really important to me all along to share my story of my treatment, my diagnosis, my treatment and my recovery, to whoever will listen, to be perfectly honest. My first desire was to tell fellow patients, and I was interviewed by a radiation oncologist. My answers to my, her questions were recorded, and those videos have been shared by doctors and other cancer team members to thousands of people who've been diagnosed with a head and neck cancer. And I'm just so grateful that clinicians have seen the value of sharing a patient's story. I think there's no substitute for a patient who's about to have radiotherapy to hear the story of a fellow patient, not only just describe what the treatment's like and the recovery's like, but just to see a patient who's survived, who's survived cancer. Because I think so many of us when we get that cancer diagnosis, we're just full of anxiety and fear, and there's nothing as reassuring as seeing a patient who's gone through it and come out the other side. But I also think it's good for cancer team members to see these videos because it, it exposes them to the emotional and psychological impact of a cancer diagnosis and the treatment. And if they can hear the patient's story, empathize, uh, understand emotionally, feel some of those feelings, I think they're much more likely to do research and make an effort to help us psychologically, which I think is as important as survival.
caption: In this audio recording, a mature female speaker with a clear Australian accent speaks passionately about the importance of sharing her experience with cancer diagnosis, treatment, and recovery. Her tone is warm, empathetic, and deeply reassuring as she describes her desire to help fellow patients overcome their anxiety and fear by seeing a survivor. She also highlights how sharing these stories can benefit cancer care teams by helping them understand the emotional and psychological impacts of the disease, potentially driving further research in psychological support. A gentle, uplifting instrumental track plays in the background, complementing her hopeful and encouraging message.

title: Acupuncture for Anxiety, Insomnia & Sports Injuries | Patient Success Story
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I've been coming to Integrative Acupuncture for 6 years now, I think. And, I've come for a variety of reasons, from injuries to anxiety to insomnia. And, it's been an amazing place. Um, I think the practitioners here are really great. I see Jen Ethridge. And, to have developed a relationship with her over the time that I've been working with her is really awesome. I think it's rare that you get to have those experiences, sort of, in the medical field um, to see somebody who has seen you for years, who you see on a regular basis, and really knows, sort of what you need to work on, what you want to work on. So, I really appreciate having a long-term um, partnership, I guess, with the practitioners here in the practice. Um, and, I mean, it's it's a very inviting environment. It's calm, it's really pleasant, everyone who works here is so lovely and helpful. And, those are things that, you know, you don't always find in the medical world, or the, you know, alternative medicine. So, that's been very appealing to me, as well. And, I kind of emerge from each session having, you get to think about what's happening because you're there, it's sort of a meditative experience. And, I think that is, is also interesting, and, and, and helpful in healing of all kinds. So, I appreciate that time, sort of, take to myself while this, the acupuncture is actually working on me, and helping solve the issues that I face. Um, yeah, I mean, I would recommend it. I think I just tried it because I'd heard many good things over the years, and read studies about how effective acupuncture could be. And, then coming here and seeing how it's helped, you know, from knee injuries and foot injuries from climbing, to me just having a lot of trouble with insomnia. Like, it's a kind of an amazing thing that it can work in so many different ways. Um, so, it was, I'm glad that I tried it, and I would recommend that other people try it, too. Yeah, I mean, as I said, I've been coming for 6 years, and would definitely continue as long as they are here. They have, the new office is really lovely, and Vanessa, who works here, she's fantastic, as well. Um, and Liza. Like, I just appreciate everybody, and will continue to come, and feel lucky that I have access to it, and am able to make use of their services.

title: Just a little flower and talk therapy for my fellow moms... #Shorts #lindseybosway
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: My two boys are napping. I have my coffee and I'm going to use just Trader Joe's flowers and make a little arrangement. Let's chat motherhood. After I had my first baby, I think looking back on it, I had more postpartum anxiety than I even knew at the time. And I did not feel like myself for like 15 months. And part of that was just like no creative drive, no desire to really do anything outside of motherhood. And when I had my second, it was definitely better, but I just remember one day he was like 12 months old and I was like, "Oh, I want to make a flower arrangement." And I was like, "Oh gosh, I'm coming back." But it is wild. So, if you're not there yet, if you just had a baby and you feel like you're not yourself, I promise it gets better. And one day you'll feel like doing something again that requires energy. But it's okay if right now you just want to nap when your baby naps. So, I just made a little grid here. That'll make it easier to stick our flowers in. And once I started doing flowers when they were napping, I feel like I have so much more energy on the days that I do it. I think it's just like using your brain for something other than motherhood, and it gives me like a jolt of energy. And often times, when we're dealing with our babies or toddlers, it's such chaos. And I just find arranging flowers to be so peaceful and meditative once you really get into it. I always think about that one creator who talks about getting her pink back. And, you know, it went viral or whatever, but it's so true. And when you're a first time mom, you have no perspective on the fact that it does come back. Your second time around is a little easier because you know what's going on, and you know that it's okay to feel that way. But it can be really jarring when you have your first baby, and you don't understand that it's temporary. It really is. Like my biggest piece of advice that I give friends is just to try to remember in motherhood that everything is temporary. It's looking really pretty, but we have a lot of space to fill in. A few finishing touches here. I also think, in motherhood, it is okay if one day you want to make this huge, amazing arrangement, and the next day you don't want to. You put your kids to bed, and you spend the next hour in your bed. It's just okay. That's how it goes. And you know what I've stopped doing? Bullying myself for that. Just let myself relax. I don't ever go to a space of shame. Because you know what's not relaxing? Sitting down, trying to relax, and worrying about the fact that you're relaxing. Here she is. She's whimsical. She's fall. I love her.

title: When My Therapist Showed Up Late .... It Made Me Notice Something About Internalizing
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hey family, just wanted to share this real quick. This may be more so a message for those who internalize. And it's something that I'm picking up on in my continuous healing work, in my own personal um journey, and just growth in general, um for people who do internalize, who could relate to this. So what I'm noticing is, is that sometimes when you internalize, it could happen very subtly. You may not even realize it. And I know I wasn't, per se, and I'll share an example, like, for instance. I had a therapist that they only have a 50-minute session when you sign up with them. And I like this therapist a lot, like I feel like I'm definitely getting work done with them, right? But I noticed that they show up late on the sessions, but they do end on time. That's a thought process, right? And it's internalizing it when I'm not willing to have the conversation with that therapist, even though I think it's something I could deal with, or maybe I think it's small, or maybe I'm trying to observe it a little bit more. To not internalize that looks like having a conversation, even if you don't think that it's a big deal, or maybe you think it is, or maybe it could be a potential problem. Not internalizing that would look like having an actual conversation. And maybe that looks like me saying, "Hey, you know, I notice that our sessions, you do um come in late. You usually start late, but you end on time, and I I feel like I'm not getting the full, you know, time." And I have a few options, right? I could even ask, "Hey, could I expect that you're going to show up late during every session? And if so, if that's something that I could expect, that you normally don't come on the sessions on time, am I going to get my full 50 minutes?" That's a part of what it would look like to not internalizing it. Instead of me just thinking it, allowing it to fester without having a conversation and allowing it to potentially become a problem where I start to feel a way inside instead of having a conversation. All right? So, just just sharing that with y'all. And maybe, you know, you'll find value in that if you are somebody who internalizes.

Number two, sitting quietly with your emotions, not avoiding them, not distracting yourself, just noticing them. Number three, asking yourself difficult but honest questions: "What triggers my stress?", "What patterns keep repeating in my life?" At American Behavioral Clinics, we believe self-awareness is one of the most important steps toward emotional wellness and personal growth. Because self-awareness isn't about perfection. It's about noticing, understanding, growing. American Behavioral Clinics, helping people better understand themselves, one step at a time.

title: The Bright Side of AI
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: With all the AI gloom and doom, I often forget how cool AI actually is. Like, what a technology, what a time to be alive. You know, like, I often have this heaviness about it, and more of this, "I gotta use this. I gotta make this work. I need to catch up with with the trends and everything, not to fall behind." And what I lose sight of sometimes is how amazing this technology is, and I just, today, I had this case of, hey, you can, you can use AI to analyze your thought patterns, like your personal thought patterns, and not only can you understand how you think, but obviously also where your blind spots are, and and how you can improve your thinking, and how, what are, what the patterns are, and this, getting this awareness about yourself, in all kinds of areas, obviously professionally, how you make decisions, but but also in private, it's such an amazing feat, to be honest. This technology didn't exist. Like, how would you else, like, get to this? Like, of course, if you do therapy for 10 years, which nobody wants, and and I'm not really a fan of it, still, there's this other person processing it, and you probably not get to the root of it. Now, you can upload hours, hundreds of hours of you interacting in in Zoom calls, whatever it is, and you can have AI analyze, find out your thought patterns, even like making your thoughts visible to yourself. And I just thought, how amazing, and this is just one use case, obviously. There's so much to be had also with this technology. It's scary. It's It puts a pressure on myself, and I guess on you as well, but it's also fabulous, and this is my, my little reminder to myself, and maybe to you, that if you, if you set aside this, this pressure, this, this fear maybe even, and and let in the, the possibilities and the opportunity a little bit more, it could be tremendously fun to interact with this technology, and and all the, the beautiful things that can come from that. See you in the next video.

title: why is it so hard to be present?

Real question is, why is this so Such a challenge for me? This This is so hard. This is so hard. I don't know. Is it a realization that maybe you don't value yourself as much as others do, or you put yourself on a higher expectation than you put others? You know, a flip would be, if this was my best friend and he did all of this, I would be so proud of him. Do I hold myself at a different standard? Why is it so hard to be present? Therefore, when I look back and reflect on it, it's something I'm a little hard on myself about. Staying present and being in that moment is really hard. And, just continue doing what you're doing. title: DEPRESSION
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You really fail. Grabe ang nadudulot ng depression sa mga tao ngayon 'no? You think I care about that? Kaya minsan hindi ko maiwasang tanungin ang sarili ko. Don't you care what people think? Doesn't it bother you that people are making you out to be a joke and that I'm being included in that? Ano nga bang pakay ko? Kasi kadalasan gusto ko lahat may aakay sa'kin. Di namamalayan sa mga tanong laging sagot, ano bang malay ko? You want to be really great? Then have the courage to fail big and stick around. Lahat 'to saan papunta? Tangina sa totoo lang hindi ko rin alam kung saan ako pupunta. Babe, that's right. Do you? Nawawalang kamalayan, ayaw maiwan, ayaw ring mauna. Ayaw kong magsimula kasi huli na ang lahat. You're better than that. You really fail. Paano pa ako papalag kung sa utak ko talo na agad? You fail, you fail, you fail, you fail, you fail. Haay. Sa bugtong hininga nalipat ang pahina. Paano pa ako magpapahinga kung 'di ko naramdaman sa bawat paghinga? Now, if you know what you're worth, then go out and get what you're worth. But you gotta be willing to take the hits. Pwede ba akong magreklamo? Saan naman ako magsusumbong? Kanino ko naman ikukuwento ang lungkot na umaalulong? Wala, 'wag na baka matawag pang mahina. Lalo na't 'di pa nakikita mga dapat kong ipakita. Try again. Fail again. Fail better. Let me tell you something you already know. The world ain't all sunshine and rainbows. It's a very mean and nasty place, and I don't care how tough you are, it will beat you to your knees and keep you there permanently if you let it. You, me, or nobody is gonna hit as hard as life. But it ain't about how hard you hit. It's about how hard you can get hit and keep moving forward; how much you can take and keep moving forward. That's how winning is done!

title: Are You Okay... Really?
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: We ask it out of habit every single day, but we rarely listen for the truth. "How are you? Are you okay?" "Yeah, I'm fine." It's the ultimate American defense mechanism. We live in a culture that glorifies the grind, praises independence, and tells us to "fake it till we make it." So when things get heavy, our language shrinks. We reduce an entire ocean of burnout, anxiety, and quiet exhaustion into a single automatic wall. "Have you been crying?" "No, just tired." "Just tired." It's the perfect cover-up. Because nobody questions it. In a world where everyone is exhausted, it's easy to hide. But there's a massive difference between needing sleep and being tired of waking up feeling empty. Depression doesn't always look like tears or dramatic breakdowns. In reality, it looks like complete isolation. It's sitting in a crowded room in New York or a quiet suburb in Ohio, surrounded by people, yet feeling entirely invisible. It's building walls so high that even the people who love you can't reach you. "Do you want to talk about it? You can tell me anything." "No, there's nothing to talk about." When someone pushes you away, it's rarely a rejection. Most of the time, they literally just don't have the words. How do you explain a profound sadness that has no specific cause? How do you tell your family or your friends that your life looks great on paper, but feels completely hollow inside? So they say "No," hoping you'll leave them alone, but secretly praying that you won't. They don't need a lecture, they don't need a motivational speech, toxic positivity, or a 10-step plan on how to fix their life. "Do you want a hug?" "Yeah." Sometimes saving a life doesn't take a hero, it doesn't take the perfect words. It just takes the willingness to sit in the dark with someone. The most powerful thing you can say to someone who is drowning isn't "I understand." It's simply, "I'm here, and you don't have to carry this alone." Right now, millions of people are fighting battles they don't talk about. And ironically, the people who spend all their energy checking on everyone else are often the ones drowning the fastest. Do me a favor today. Don't just send a casual text asking "How's it going?" Call someone, look them in the eyes, break through the automatic answers. Because you never truly know how heavy a burden is until you offer to help hold it. Check on your people today.

His voice is calm, warm, and deeply expressive, spoken with a slow, deliberate pace that allows each word to resonate. A soft, melancholic piano melody plays continuously in the background, enhancing the emotional depth and sincere tone of the narration. The speaker discusses how common phrases like "I'm fine" and "just tired" are often used as defense mechanisms to hide deep-seated anxiety, depression, and exhaustion. He encourages listeners to move beyond casual check-ins, call their loved ones, and offer genuine presence and support, noting that sometimes saving a life simply requires sitting with someone in their darkness. The audio is clean and intimate, with well-balanced sound design.

title: Inside the Mind of Someone Who Feels Alone | Deep Narration About Loneliness
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Sometimes the loneliest feeling isn't when you're alone, it's when you're surrounded by people and still feel like you don't belong. The room is full of voices, laughter, conversations, noise, but somehow, none of it reaches you. You smile when they look at you, you nod like you're listening, you say you're fine, because it's easier than explaining what's going on inside your head. Sometimes you hold your phone, staring at the screen, wanting to text someone, but not knowing who would understand. You start typing, then delete everything, because how do you explain a feeling you don't even understand yourself? Outside, the world keeps moving. People walk with purpose, cars pass by. Everyone seems to be going somewhere. And you wonder why you feel stuck in the same place, every single day. Loneliness isn't always silence. Sometimes it's noise that doesn't include you. Sometimes it's laughing with people, but feeling nothing inside. Sometimes it's going home and realizing, no one really knows how you feel. You sit in your room, the lights are off. The only sound is your own thoughts, and they don't stop. You ask yourself questions: Why do I feel like this? Why can't I connect? Why does everything feel so far away? But even on days like this, when the silence feels too loud, a small part of you is still there. Still breathing, still trying, still hoping. And sometimes, that's enough. Sometimes, making it through the day while feeling alone is already a victory. And maybe tomorrow feels lighter. Maybe not easier, but a little less heavy. title: Why Smaller Gifts Mean Big Potential
transcription: Over 50 million transactions were analyzed across 1,000 non-profit organizations globally in 2025. So that means that what we're seeing is actual donor behavior, and that's what we're going to talk about today. So what we found in all of this data is this big paradox. The average one-time gift size actually declined by 1% and the average monthly gift size in the US declined by almost 5.5%. Now that can set off some alarm bells, but here's the paradox. Uh conversion rates are rising. Uh recurring enrollment is growing up to 9% and mobile donations crossed uh 50% threshold. Social to recurring conversion doubled in email. Um what does all this mean? Well, I wanted to start by just kind of researching what other paradoxes are out there and are there any similar ones? Uh and forgive the like little history lesson here, but I found this super interesting. Uh there's this thing called the Jevons paradox. Uh back in the 1800s, this guy William Jevons, he noticed that when steam engines were getting much more efficient, right? We like crossed this threshold where steam engines were getting super super efficient. So the hypothesis was, hey, we're going to use less coal. Well, what happened was people didn't use less coal, the tech was so good that there were more and more steam engines. So everybody got a steam engine and total coal use exploded, right? So how does that relate to this? Well, we're seeing the exact same thing in fundraising right now. As the friction of giving goes down, the initial cost of entry is smaller. The volume of committed donors is really booming. And so donors aren't pulling back, they're moving faster, committing a little bit differently. Smaller upfront gifts don't necessarily mean lower donor value. Organizations that are winning in 2026 will build their revenue architecture around how donors are actually giving today. And from what we've seen in this data, it's mobile-first, it's social-driven, and also commitment-led.

title: PART 4 | How to Pitch Climate Innovation to Investors | The Art of Storytelling
transcription: or tell the story that sells, because let's face it, none of this matters if you can't bring people on board. Intensive pitch clinics break their coaching down into three aggressive phases. First, you spend 20 minutes getting inspired by great storytelling. Then, you face a grueling 60 minutes actively drafting your pitch. Finally, you spend 20 minutes reflecting and absorbing some brutal, yet constructive, peer feedback. The whole point is to aggressively transition dense academic research into actionable, exciting storytelling. When you're presenting your climate innovation to investors, keep this quote in mind. Clarity helps to convey complex ideas simply. Remember, investors are not grading your thesis. They're evaluating a business opportunity. Absolute clarity will always heavily outweigh dense, overwhelming data. If they don't get it in the first 2 minutes, honestly, the pitch is over. So, your pitch has to be laser-focused. It needs to concisely articulate a compelling problem, followed by your robust solution. You have to clearly define your specific target market and the measurable environmental and economic impact. And finally, you need a crystal clear ask, like exactly how much money do you need, and what milestones will it unlock, along with how you clearly differentiate from competitors. Keep the whole shebang tight. So, we'll leave you with this defining challenge. Will your hard-fought climate innovation become just another one of those 95% of inactive patents gathering dust? Or, will you master this playbook, bridge the gap, and build exactly what the market is desperately waiting for? The ecosystem needs your solutions right now. It's up to you to deliver them. Thanks for joining me for this Explainer, and keep innovating.

title: The Foundry Pitch Competition Informational Video
transcription: Before starting Amplab, I definitely was the type of person to not go outside the box and kind of just do what was asked of me. But then coming to Amplab and having my brother be here before, I kind of saw how important it is to step outside the box to get something out of Amplab. You have access to so many connections and like a huge network here, it's crazy. So using that network to really help set your business apart was a big thing for me. So here at Amplab, they focus on problem-solving a lot. You need to have a problem to be able to come up with solutions. So I looked into my own life and kind of took my love for animals a part of that and saw my dog was having issues with nutrition and saw how big of a role nutrition actually plays in pets' lives. So I saw his food allergies and his skin issues and how they were connected, so I wanted to create a pet food business that focused on the customization of nutrition and showed how high-quality ingredients can really help with that. So preparing for the Foundry was a lot, but it was very empowering. We spent a couple weeks working on our pitch, which was five minutes long, and then we also prepared for the Q&A that the judges did. And with that, we just asked each other questions and prepared that way. My business, Tailored Bites, that me and my business partner worked on, we also competed in Innovate WithIn, so we used a lot of our Foundry prize money towards that competition. So a lot of it went to ingredients so we created a bunch of food to sell at the Fort Wayne Farmers Market that is right here by Amplab. So a lot of it was ingredients to make the meals. We had a human-grade chicken dog food. We also prepped the judges' food for the Innovate WithIn contest and created custom lunch boxes with our food in it. So anyways, without further ado, the winner of the first-ever Foundry pitch competition, Tailored Bites. I would say really put your best effort. It is really rewarding to see it all come together at the competition like seeing the months of preparation come out and to be able to show it to your family and friends and also community members is really impactful.

transcription: The CompSci Pitch Comp is a completely new competition at UNSW. It's the first time undergraduate students get an opportunity to pitch to the UNSW Investment Committee for a real investment. It's usually a right that is reserved to to staff at UNSW or to post-graduate students in special circumstances, um but it's never been done before for undergraduate students. Classroom performance can only do so much when it comes to assessing the talent, the grit, and the creativity of our students. Before it was sort of assumed that like, you know, the students wouldn't have anything mature enough to to be able to fund or or the ideas would be too nascent or whatever. But what we've discovered is that, you know, um there are some great ideas and they're quite mature as well. So I'm really excited to to go a bit further on that. Every 11 minutes in Australia, someone suffers a stroke, which means by the time we wrap up the two next pitches tonight, someone's life will change completely. I I remember growing up and feeling like sort of powerless to the world and like the whims of how things were happening around me. But I'm very excited to be able to do something that I think can actually make an impact. It's actually one of our biggest milestones to just being able to pitch to investors and really learn from their opinions and be able to take this even further. This opportunity means a lot to us, because not only the money, right, but also where it's coming from, like, startups, yeah, UNSW Founders has dealt with thousands of startups that have faced the exact issues we are trying to mediate for people. title: The 5 Things Angel Investors Look for Before They Invest
transcription: How angel investors actually decide to invest. Imagine you've spent months, maybe even years, building your startup. You finally get a meeting with an angel investor. You walk in, deliver what you think is the perfect pitch, and they pass. So what happened? The truth is, angel investors aren't just investing in ideas. They're investing in founders. They're investing in execution. And most importantly, they're investing in the probability that your business can succeed. Here are the five things they're really looking for. First, the founder. This is by far the most important factor. Investors know that startups rarely go exactly according to plan. Markets change, products evolve, and unexpected problems come up all the time. They're asking themselves one simple question: Can this founder figure it out? A great founder is resilient, adaptable, and able to execute even when things don't go as planned. Second, the problem. Is it a real problem that people genuinely want solved? Or is it just a nice idea? The bigger and more painful the problem, the more valuable the solution becomes. Great businesses solve expensive problems, not minor inconveniences. Third, the market. Even an incredible product has limited potential if it's built for a tiny audience. Investors look for large growing markets because they want companies that can scale. If the opportunity isn't big enough, neither is the return. Fourth, traction. One of the biggest myths is that you need massive revenue before investors will take you seriously. That's simply not true. What investors really want is evidence that people care. That could be growing users, paying customers, partnerships, a waiting list, or strong engagement. Any sign that the market is responding positively reduces the risk of investing. And finally, why you? What's stopping another company from copying your idea tomorrow? Maybe it's your experience, maybe it's your technology, your network, your community, or simply your ability to execute faster than everyone else. The strongest startups don't just have a great idea. They have a compelling reason why they're the best team to bring that idea to life. At the end of the day, angel investing is all about reducing risk. Every customer you gain, every milestone you hit, and every problem you solve gives investors one more reason to believe. Because investors don't invest in certainty, they invest in confidence. title: Choosing the Wrong Person to Pitch Your Startup | Chinese Competition Reality
transcription: A lot of international entrepreneurs, they underestimate how important the applicant actually is for Chinese startup competitions. The applicant can make or break the deal. You can either succeed through this or you just fail. We had startups that applied twice to one competition, one year one applicant, the other year another applicant, and we figured out that it is extremely important who applies and the background of the applicant. Some startups, they choose to let an intern or a manager apply to the competition, but the problem here is that they do not have the relevant background to get through the entire process. What Chinese startup competitions usually want to see is the CEO or at least C-level applicants that have a substantial amount of equity in the startup. There are certain startup competitions, usually most of the competitions, they require at least 30% of equity in the startup. Not at this time, but usually in the process of the establishment of the startup, you should have had at one point 30% of equity. There are some competitions that do not require this. We usually highlight this in the process of supporting you to get through the startup competition, but these competitions are usually rare. And sometimes it's not really important that the CEO applies, because if your education background is not top-notch, so you don't have a master degree or a PhD, then maybe another person of your business should apply to the competition. Because usually the higher the the degree, the better the chances of getting through. So, if you have someone in your team that you can trust with the establishment of the entity in China, then you could choose a PhD manager in your company to apply to this competition. Also, please be aware that the applicant has to usually pitch through the entire process of the competition, which is usually the preliminary round, the semi-finals, the final, and usually you also have to come to China to receive the prize. So education background is extremely important, the amount of equity in the startup is extremely important, and also the relevant background is important. So if you're in biotech, but you do not have a biotech background, so you don't have a university degree in this, then it's very hard for you to get through. One plus that you can do is, if you have a Chinese team member, you can let them apply to the competition, because then usually the trust of the judges of you succeeding in the Chinese market is also higher. But if you don't have that, that's not a problem. Usually choose the one with the highest university degree and with the highest amount of shares, and make sure that this person can be and will be in China if you win a good amount, and if you can come to China. If you want to increase your chances of winning at a Chinese startup competition, reach out to us. We have helped thousands of startups to land substantial winning prizes from all different regions of the world. Subscribe to the channel to get more updates, give us a like if you also liked the content of the video, and if you want to get support in your next application, just write in the comments and we will reach out to you. Thank you for watching, and see you in the next video.

title: Why Didn't Robinhood Blame AI for Layoffs?
transcription: Why didn't Robinhood blame AI for layoffs? Robinhood is still cutting about 290 jobs, even as the company reports growth, and CEO Vlad Tenev left AI out of the memo entirely. That omission is the story, because plenty of tech companies now use AI as the reason for shrinking teams. The layoff note came from CEO Vlad Tenev, and he did something unusual for a tech chief right now. He made no mention of AI. That matters because Robinhood is not hiding behind a productivity story. The company is still shrinking its workforce while saying the business is growing, so the message is blunt. The cuts are about the company's structure, not a public AI excuse. That silence stands out because many tech companies have started using AI language in layoff announcements. Amazon, Block, Coinbase, GitLab, and Intuit have all used similar logic around leaner teams, less bureaucracy, and fewer silos. Robinhood chose not to join that script. Instead, the note pointed away from AI and toward a broader internal reset. That analyst view reinforces the point. According to Citizens JMP Securities analyst Devin Ryan, AI-driven efficiency was not the main driver of the reduction, because Robinhood has long been aggressively leveraging artificial intelligence across the organization. In other words, if AI was already part of the machine, it could not be the easy excuse for the cuts. The company's internal message had to point somewhere else. This is why the Robinhood memo is getting attention beyond one company. Tech firms are under pressure to justify layoffs at the same time AI tools are being sold as efficiency machines. Robinhood's choice suggests that the AI blame game may be losing credibility fast. If a company already uses AI broadly, saying AI caused the cuts starts to sound like a cover story, not an explanation. Robinhood cut 10% of its staff, about 290 jobs, but skipped the AI script that many peers now lean on. The real takeaway is simple. Companies are being pushed to explain restructuring more directly, especially when AI is already part of their operations.

title: The Perfect 60-Second Startup Pitch (Investors Will Remember)
transcription: The perfect 60-second startup pitch. Imagine you step into an elevator with your dream investor. You have exactly 60 seconds before the doors open. Would you know what to say? Most founders make one big mistake. They try to explain everything about their business. The truth is, your goal isn't to close the investment in 60 seconds. It's to make the investor want another conversation. Here's a simple framework that works. First, start with the problem. What pain are you solving? Keep it simple and relatable. If the investor doesn't understand the problem, they won't care about the solution. Next, explain your solution. In one sentence, describe what your company does. Avoid technical jargon or long explanations. If someone outside your industry can't understand it, it's probably too complicated. Then, explain why now. Why is this the right time for your business? Maybe a new technology has made your solution possible. Maybe customer behavior has changed. Maybe the market is growing rapidly. Investors want to know why this opportunity exists today, not 5 years ago. After that, share your traction. You don't need millions in revenue, but you do need evidence that you're making progress. That could be paying customers, user growth, partnerships, pilot programs, or even a growing waitlist. Traction reduces uncertainty and builds confidence. Finally, finish with the opportunity. Don't end by asking for money. Instead, leave the investor wanting to learn more. Give them a reason to schedule a second meeting. Remember, a great pitch doesn't answer every question. It answers just enough to create curiosity. If an investor walks away wanting to know more, you've done your job. The best founders don't overwhelm investors with information. They tell a clear story, communicate confidence, and make their business easy to understand. Because at the end of the day, investors don't invest in the longest pitch, they invest in the clearest one. title: My 90 Second Beverage Pitch for the TCU Venture Competition
transcription: Hi, my name is Carl Gunther. I'm the founder of Seven Castle Cider. We are a beverage company from Western New York producing non-alcoholic sparkling apple cider made from our locally sourced upcycled apples that would otherwise be thrown out. Our flagship product is a modern 12 oz can made with just fresh apple juice and carbonation. No artificial additives, no added sugars, no preservatives, none of that nonsense. The non-alcoholic beverage industry is growing rapidly, but sparkling cider is being left out. Most options are seasonal, sold in large bottles, or made from concentrate. Seven Castle Cider reimagines cider as a year-round, everyday social beverage, something that belongs at dinners, weddings, celebrations, gatherings, parties, anything without alcohol being a barrier. Our mission is to create inclusive social spaces while also helping the environment and our local economy. Whether someone doesn't drink for health, faith, or personal reasons, they still deserve a drink to feel celebratory. We validated this demand through in-person tastings, parties, and over 200,000 organic social media views before launch. Operationally, we are ready to launch. We have our scheduled processes all complete. We have one last inspection for our 20-C commercial production license, and we have our sales tax authority for New York State. We are also in the talks with local co-packers so we can get our beverage produced at large scales through them. We have MSRP at 2.99 can, which gives us room for profits and growth. We are bootstrapped, we are value-driven, and we are built for sustainable growth, and we are not just a beverage. We are selling a more inclusive way for people to gather. title: Inside the VC Mindset: What Makes a Pitch Win
transcription: Hi everyone, this is Jaden Chow. Welcome to the Shark Tank PHS virtual club space. Today we're answering an important question. What is crucial if you want a VC to fund your business idea? First, what is a VC? VC stands for Venture Capitalist. A VC is someone who gives money to new businesses they believe can grow big. Instead of getting paid back like a loan, they receive part ownership of the business. If the business succeeds, they succeed, too. Because of that, VCs don't invest in just any idea. They invest in ideas that are clear, realistic, and ready to grow. That's where the winning pitch formula comes in. First is the problem. You must clearly explain a real pain point people actually have. Second, the solution. What is your product or service, and how does it work? Third, the value proposition. Why is your solution better or different from others? Fourth, the market. Who is this for, and how many people need it? Fifth, the business model. How does your idea make money? Next is traction. This is proof that people want your idea, like users, sales, or strong interest. Then comes competition. Other solutions exist. Explain who they are, and why your idea can win. Next are financials. You don't need perfect numbers, but you need to show you understand costs and revenue. Then there's the ask. How much money are you asking for, and what are you offering in return? Finally, vision and scale. Show how your idea can grow bigger in the future. If you can clearly explain all 10 of these, a VC is much more likely to listen. Thanks for watching. See you in the next lesson.

He systematically breaks down the pitch into ten key elements: identifying a clear problem, presenting a solution, defining the value proposition, identifying the market, explaining the business model, showing traction, acknowledging competition, outlining financials, making the ask, and demonstrating vision and scale. transcription: In front. Okay. Given that there's money movement involved here, can you talk a little bit about any risk that is associated with the transactions that occur? Certainly, there's always risk when you move money, but we don't hold the money. We only tell the money what to do. The money is still held inside of a bank or other money-lending institution that is fully licensed, FDIC, OCC regulated, all that is still there. None of those things change. We're simply telling it when to move. What about the verification of those milestones, and who decides yes, this milestone has been completed, therefore we can move the funds out of the escrow account and to the contractor? How is that determined? Great question. It's set up by the owner of the project, the person who's got the money, who is paying to have the work done. They put their criteria into the system, and then when, if I'm, again, the plumber, and I win the bid, I agree to that system. And then, when those milestones are met, the plumber says, "Hey, I'm done." Yes, that's set up, but it's the owner that retains complete control throughout the whole process. Thank you. So, um, I can understand why the subcontractor would want this to get paid more quickly. But why would the contractor, what's the, uh, the rationale for why they would want to adopt this? Uh, number of reasons, and thank you very much for the question. 14% is why. The average cost of construction projects on, on average in 2024, and I'll be happy to show you more of that in the, in detail on the side, but in 2024, the average cost of every construction project is up by 14% based on this issue, and that is slow pay, that is cost of carry, that is legal issues from mechanics liens, and such. So, they want to do that. The second reason why they want to do that is because good help is hard to find. There is an increasing amount of work happening, and less and less people to do the work, and good help is hard to find. So, if you are the contractor who pays on time, good help is not going to be nearly as hard to find. What's your, uh, market validation or traction today? We are testing our MVP as we speak. We are going to go into our beta test next month. We assume our beta test will be complete come June 1st, and then we're going to go live. In the meantime, we've got a long list of people that we have been talking with. We've got a long list of people who are excited about this. I can't say who they are yet, right? But we have a long list of people ready to go once we're ready to go. How do you defend, um, the current existing project management software from making something similar and basically bolting it on to their existing solutions? Great question. So, let's say, for example, a Procore, right, an existing project management software company, decides to bolt this on and create this themselves. They can, and it will be very successful for them if they're smart enough to do it. The problem is that's just for the Procore customers. It's not industry-wide like we are. So, they're going to have a limited market space, and we have the entire market space. And you can have more than one in there. There's four engines. Thank you. Thank you.

title: States scramble to redistrict after Supreme Court limits Voting Rights Act
transcription:
Tonight, new political turmoil. Alabama and Tennessee are the latest states rushing to redraw congressional districts after a Supreme Court ruling that further weakened voting rights. CBS News Congressional Correspondent Nicole Killion has the latest. Nicole.

Six months out from the midterms and the redistricting wars are intensifying for control of Congress after a recent Supreme Court ruling rolled back a key part of the Voting Rights Act. The Supreme Court's 6-to-3 decision to strike down Louisiana's congressional map hits right in the heart of Cleo Fields' seat. The district was created, first of all, Louisiana's minority population, black population, is over a third of the state. The Democrat represents the sixth congressional district, which slinks from Shreveport to Baton Rouge. But the high court ruled the newly drawn majority-minority district was an unconstitutional gerrymander since it was based on race. Congressman Troy Carter represents the other majority-minority district in New Orleans. It can wipe out both of our seats. We can, realistically, end up having six congressional districts with no African-American or Democratic representation. Ahead of early voting this weekend, Louisiana officials suspended House primary elections slated for November until the state can redraw its map. I don't think that it's going to result in a loss of minority representation, and I think that we have to give the—the people a chance to draw their districts the way the people want to see them drawn. Before the Supreme Court ruling, at least seven states had already passed new congressional maps as part of mid-decade redistricting. Now, several Southern states are using the High Court's decision to justify changes before the midterms, including Florida, Alabama, and Tennessee. It was really not about, you know, that little seat in Louisiana. It's about redistricting all over the nation. It's about the voting rights of people all over the nation. While these new moves by Southern states could potentially net more Republican seats, Democrats are vowing to fight back and are looking to other blue states that could possibly change their maps in the 2028 cycle. Jericka. Nicole Killion, thank you so much.

title: Supreme Court appears skeptical of mail-in ballots that arrive after Election Day
transcription: The Supreme Court just finished hearing arguments in a major case that raises questions about the legality of mail-in voting. And the conservative justices appeared skeptical about allowing states to count ballots that are mailed on time, but arrive after Election Day. The court's ruling could upend the voting process in more than a dozen states just months before this November's midterm elections. NBC News legal affairs reporter Gary Grumbach joins us now. So, Gary, this case stems from an election law in Mississippi, so walk us through it and what we've heard so far from the justices. Yeah, the oral arguments were supposed to be about whether postmarked ballots by Election Day could be accepted after Election Day, but it really turned into a debate on a variety of different election-related topics, from who is actually delivering that ballot to the state, topics about like ballot harvesting, to conversations about potentially people being able to recall their votes. For example, if you were to send something in via FedEx, could you tell FedEx, "Oh no, I actually want that back"? And then there was conversations about the length of time the state allows a voter to be able to get their ballot in and have it count. So, for example, some states do a week, some states do 21 days. Conservative Justice Samuel Alito, predictably, was pretty upset about all of this. He said, "We used to have Election Day, now it's election month or election months," guys. Gary, if the Supreme Court does rule in favor of the RNC and Mississippi's GOP, what does that essentially mean more broadly for the rest of the country when it comes to these midterms? So, Mississippi was the state that was arguing this and defending their own law, but there's 13 other states that have similar laws, so this would be a very significant thing for almost half the country here in terms of whether or not ballots would be allowed to be counted after Election Day. You have a map there that shows states, both red and blue states, that we're looking at there. And it also specifically relates to some of these military ballots, right? Folks that are serving overseas in our military, especially right now, uh may not be able to get their ballots in on time even though they are postmarked by Election Day. We will have to see exactly how the justices write this opinion, which we should be getting it by the end of June. We thank you for watching, and remember, stay updated on breaking news and top stories on the NBC News app or watch live on our YouTube channel.

title: Supreme Court weakens the Voting Rights Act after 61 years
transcription: The US Supreme Court dealt a blow to the landmark Voting Rights Act on Wednesday after knocking out a major pillar of the law that had protected against racial discrimination in voting and representation. In the six decades since it was signed, the Voting Rights Act became one of the most consequential laws in the nation's history, preventing discrimination against minorities at the ballot box. It also helped elect Black and Hispanic representatives at all levels of government. But on Wednesday, the Supreme Court hollowed out the landmark civil rights era law by striking down a majority Black congressional district in Louisiana. That ruling could provide an open door for political mapmakers to undermine minority representation. The Voting Rights Act was signed into law by President Lyndon B. Johnson on August 6, 1965, five months after the Bloody Sunday attack on civil rights marchers in Selma, Alabama, gave momentum to the bill. Wherever there is discrimination, this law will strike down all restrictions used to deny the people the right to vote. In recent years, AP reporter Gary Fields sat down with some of the people who were pivotal to the birth of the Act. After having talked to these individuals and to a number of other people about why voting rights was so important, the reason for why they were so important then hasn't changed now. In a democracy or a republic such as ourselves, the vote is the thing that you have that is the coin of the realm that allows you to say I'm a full participant in this society, in this endeavor that we call the United States of America. The question now is what comes next for minority representatives and the communities they represent.

title: Supreme Court Steps In After Judge Orders Trump Arrested Live—Emergency Appeal Changes Everything.
transcription:
The sealed 94-page leak: What nobody is connecting yet.

A sealed 94-page federal grand jury transcript leaked Tuesday night, and the legal fallout is already escalating. Federal grand jury testimony is classified as secret under Rule 6 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, meaning this document was never supposed to exist in the public domain. Yet, at 11:47 p.m. on Tuesday, the full unredacted transcript hit ProPublica's servers. Someone on the inside broke protocol to leak it, which is a federal felony in itself. However, the true significance lies within the contents of the testimony, specifically, brand new sworn statements provided by former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson during an undisclosed session in January 2026. Unlike her previous public appearances, this fourth session under oath involved different prosecutors, different targets, and crucial documentary evidence. On page 12 of the transcript, when asked if she maintained personal knowledge of White House communications, Hutchinson revealed that she kept a personal record comprising text message screenshots, calendar entries, and three handwritten journals. Because these were maintained as personal records, rather than official government property, they fall outside standard executive privilege claims and cannot be shielded as easily. Hutchinson essentially created her own paper trail, which has now become central to the prosecution's case. The transcript lays out a detailed timeline of post-election strategy. Page 18 introduces Exhibit 47, a November 9, 2024, text message from Mark Meadows instructing Hutchinson to establish a direct line with former DOJ official Jeffrey Clark and then Michigan Senate Majority Leader Mike Shirkey. Page 23 details a November 11th conference call arranged by Hutchinson featuring Donald Trump, Mark Meadows, Jeffrey Clark, Mike Shirkey, Rudy Giuliani, an Arizona State Senator, and Hutchinson herself. According to her testimony, the explicit topic of the call was developing strategies to delay election certification in Michigan and Arizona, focusing directly on disrupting the certification process, rather than pursuing standard court challenges.

title: How Indie Creators Are Building Shows With Shorts
transcription: Vertical short-form animation used to feel to me like this weird side quest. Like something you did for the algorithm, but not for your actual career. But lately, I've been seeing indie animators use shorts to quietly build entire worlds. Characters, shows, fan bases, momentum. So today, I want to break down the storytelling formats that are actually working and how you can use them for your own projects. Because here's the truth: most of us don't get to make a full series right away. We don't get handed a season order and a budget and a team. We build things slowly. And shorts are how a lot of creators are doing that right now. They help you test ideas, grow an audience, prove there's really something there. They're not throwaway content. They're like micro-pilots, proof of concepts. I've been doing this storytelling thing for a while now, in studios and independently. And the creators who are really winning in short form aren't just posting random clips. They're actually telling tiny, strategic stories. Hi, I'm Emily Brundige, and I create cartoons for a living. Over the past decade, I've pitched and sold eight original animated shows. Most recently, I created my own original animated show, Goldie, for Apple TV. It's been nominated for two Emmys, including Best Writing. When I look at the shorts that turn into long-term fandoms, I see the same three storytelling models that really work. They seem simple, but structurally, they're doing something very smart. Let's start with the most classic storytelling format. Self-contained stories. Mummy Joe is a great example of this. Every short is its own tiny episode: beginning, middle, and end. Nothing carries over, so you can click on any one, and you're not lost, you're just in. Why does this work? You don't need context, you don't need lore. You just click and you're watching a whole story. You feel satisfied.

title: [HIGHLIGHT] How DEVO Created the “Whip It” Sound (The Real Story) - From EP 379
transcription: Robert Margouleff is memoir Shaping Sounds, Stevie Wonder, DEVO, the Synth Revolution and My Life Behind the Music. You describe DEVO as wanting to put an alien head on an R&B body. What did that phrase mean to you in, in musical terms? Well, uh, just as a quick aside, the thing is this, the, the DEVOs love R&B. They grew up listening to R&B. So when I came on board, I made really sure that the bottom end of their records was really R&B. There was, the band was a small band. It was not meant to have lots of overdubs. It was, should be, it was a simple band. Everyone played their part, one part each, right? When they played together, it was an ensemble. But it was more like a string quartet. It was tight and it was together, but it had an R&B bottom end. And I made very sure that that stuck, that the bottom end, the kick in the bass, were the R&B, had the R&B feel. And then they put the, the monster on the top. But it was an R&B body with a, with an alien head. That's what DEVO is. Yeah. When you first heard it, do-do-do-do-do, ping, dow, were you thinking? Five up, two down. Da-da-da-da-da, five notes. Bam-bam, two notes down. Very simple, very easy to remember, very impulsive feel. Those guys are marvelous. Mark is a marvelous songwriter. Jerry knows how to really write the lyrics. Jerry is a real politician. And you know, he just had a baby last year or the year before. And he's, He's pushing 70. But they also had that genius in the idea of the, uh, image, you know, the look. Yeah. When you look at their live show, you can, when you look at their live show, you really realize how really tight and highly organized they are. They are absolute geniuses at this stuff. All we had to do is just not drip stuff all over them, sugar coating and syrup and bullshit, and just let them play their instruments and play out, and maintain their impulsive energy. And by bringing them into the control room, I was able to do that, and allow the cross talk and the energy and everything else to really fulfill itself, super loud and quad in the control room.

title: Audio Files: Lessons NOT YET Learned
transcription: The Tech on Demand podcast brought to you by GrowerTalks. Audio Files Episode 76. Lessons Not Yet Learned. From the February 2026 issue of Green Profit magazine, written by Bill McCurry, narrated by Bill Calkins. Lessons Not Yet Learned. Philip quadrupled his dad's operations during his 23-year term as CEO. He invested in new operations, dramatically improving results. At 46, Philip died unexpectedly. Alex, his 20-year-old son, assumed control of the organization. Not everyone felt this was the right choice. Alex dismissed those who wouldn't get on board. He wisely continued the investments in new technology, results in even greater success than his father had achieved. By the time of Alex's unforeseen death at 33, the organization was 10 times the size it had been at his father's death. 5 years later, that organization had deteriorated to substantially smaller than when Philip ran it. Alex was toasted and written about as one of the greatest leaders in history. He was probably the first PR-based autocratic personality with no true leadership beyond misleading publicity and fear. Beginning in 343 BC, Aristotle tutored Alex for 3 years. Today we call him Alexander the Great. Based on the outcomes for his organization, team, and citizens, he should be called Alexander the Goof. At his deathbed, generals asked Alexander, "Who shall lead us?" Alexander replied, "Whoever is the strongest." The reality is Alexander would leave behind only fighters and no trained leaders. None of the generals were taught anything but rampaging, knocking heads, and killing. They had no understanding of negotiation, compromise, or leadership. The generals fought each other for elevation to Alexander's position. As a result, that era's Greek empire withered away in civil wars, rebellions, disintegration, and loss of power and influence. Alexander didn't expect to die young and didn't plan or train for succession. His leadership style was complete control. He neither trained his possible successors nor shared any information with them. His iron-handed rule gave no thought for the future.

title: World's First Car | Who invented the Car? | History of the Automobile Invention | Dr. Binocs Show
transcription: Oh, are you enjoying the race, little kitty? Absolutely, it's amazing. Salute to the person who invented the first car. Well, not exactly. The car wasn't invented by just one person. It was actually the result of a long, competitive race between inventors, all trying to build the future. Let's travel back in time and explore the story behind one big question: who invented the car? Zoom in! The story starts in 1769 with a French engineer named Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot, who built what is widely considered the first self-propelled vehicle. It was a steam-powered machine designed to haul cannons for the French army. It worked... sort of. It was slow, heavy, and even crashed into a wall during a demonstration. Still, it proved something revolutionary: vehicles didn't need horses to move. This idea sparked a technological race, as inventors across Europe experimented with steam, electricity, and eventually, gasoline. The real breakthrough came later in the 19th century with the development of the internal combustion engine, an engine that burns fuel like gasoline to create motion. This changed everything. Instead of bulky steam engines, vehicles could now be smaller, faster, and more efficient. That's when Carl Benz, a German engineer, entered the race. In 1885...

title: Scientists studied doomscrolling. Here’s what they found.
transcription:
What does the science actually say about whether social media is ruining our attention spans? Personally, I'm finding it a lot harder these days to sit down and read a book or watch a movie without scrolling on my phone, and it's those short vertical videos that feel particularly addicting. So, how much of that is my ability to focus actually getting worse versus me just worrying about losing my attention span? All of these fears are fairly new, so there's not a ton of high-quality studies that have been done, but there are a few. And recently, the science YouTuber, Joss Fong, posted a really great explanation on her channel, How To, where she dove into what the existing science can tell us about whether that brain rot is real, or if it's all just in our fearful heads.

In this conversation about attention spans, there's a phrase that I keep hearing, which is "brain rot". What do we actually mean by that phrase "brain rot"? What are we actually thinking is happening to ourselves and what is happening to ourselves?

I think what people mostly mean when they talk about brain rot is a kind of low-quality internet content on mostly algorithmic social media feeds, probably primarily these short-form video feeds, but also things like on Reddit or Twitter. I think people imply a low quality, but also they're implying a certain effect that they have on, that this is having on our minds.

So it's the content and the impact of the content.

I think so, yeah. And, and for me the question has been, if I'm spending more and more of my life consuming this kind, this kind of media, is that having an impact on my brain? And I think what we hear from a lot of people is, "I used to be able to read books and now I can't. I used to be able to watch movies, um, and now I can't." And so the implication with brain rot is that it's not just our environment changing and the fact that we have this device that's constantly distracting us, but there's actually a change happening in our brains. And that was the question that I really wanted to chase down, is whether that's actually true.

So, you went digging into an enormous amount of research, and I love what you found, because there are actually people who have done scientific studies, rather than just us thinking this is our perception, they've actually gone through and they've kind of measured what is happening. Um

title: Cessna Crash Layton Utah, Southwest Flight 512 Honolulu Diversion, Beijing Tower Crash Deliberate
transcription: Welcome to Aviator DB News Briefing. Today is Sunday, August 2nd, 2026. Here are today's top stories. Layton, Utah plane crash, two hospitalized after Cessna flips on SR-193. Southwest flight medical emergency diverts flight 512 back to Honolulu. FAA launches science-based marijuana fitness review for pilots, controllers. Beijing tower crash was deliberate, Chinese authorities confirm. Now for the details. Two people were hospitalized in stable condition after a small plane crash landed and flipped on State Route 193 near Fort Lane in Layton, Utah, late July 31st, 2026. The incident occurred shortly before midnight adjacent to Hill Air Force Base, KHIF, according to reports from KUTV and KSL. Emergency responders from the Layton Fire Department said the aircraft, identified as a Cessna 172, lost altitude rapidly before the engine cut out, then landed on the highway and flipped inverted. Both the pilot and passenger self-extricated from the wreckage before being transported to a local hospital. Crews contained a fuel spill at the scene, and no post-crash fire occurred. Layton police said the aircraft likely departed from Ogden and may have been attempting to land at Hill Air Force Base when the accident happened. Authorities told Univision that wind may have been a contributing factor, though the precise cause remains undetermined. The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board, NTSB, have been notified and are leading the investigation. This incident follows a series of recent general aviation accidents in Utah, including a fatal Cessna 172S crash in Box Elder County and an emergency landing near Smithfield. The NTSB typically releases preliminary findings within two weeks. Final reports can take significantly longer. A passenger medical emergency forced Southwest Flight 512 to return to Honolulu on Tuesday night after departing for San Diego. The aircraft had left Hawaii around 9:00 p.m. when crew declared an emergency following an undisclosed medical issue aboard.

transcription: ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിലേക്ക് വരുന്നതിൽ ബാഴ്സലോണ പേടിക്കണം എന്ന് പറയുന്നവരുണ്ടല്ലോ. ശരിക്കും ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോ വരുന്ന ഈ വർഷം, അതായത് 2023 മുതൽ നോക്കുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ ഒരു ചരിത്രത്തിനെയൊക്കെ അടിസ്ഥാനപ്പെടുത്തിയാണ് നമ്മൾ സംസാരിക്കാൻ പോകുന്നത്. ആദ്യമേ പേടിക്കണോ എന്ന് ചോദിച്ചു കഴിഞ്ഞാൽ നമ്മൾ ഹിസ്റ്ററിയെ ബേസ് ചെയ്തിട്ടുള്ള ഒരു കാര്യമാണ് പറയാനായിട്ട് പോകുന്നത്. ഇതിങ്ങനെയൊക്കെ തന്നെ സംഭവിക്കണം എന്ന് നിർബന്ധമൊന്നുമില്ലെങ്കിലും പലപ്പോഴും ഫുട്ബോളിൽ ഈ ചരിത്രമാവർത്തിക്കുകയാണല്ലോ എന്ന് പറയുന്ന പോലെ ഒരു സംഭവത്തെക്കുറിച്ചാണ് നമ്മൾ പറയാൻ പോകുന്നത്. ബാഴ്സലോണ ശരിക്കും ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയെ പേടിക്കണോ? ഇതാണ് ടോപ്പിക്. അപ്പൊ എന്തായാലും നമ്മൾ വിഷയം വിഷയമായിട്ട് സംസാരിക്കുന്നതിനു മുൻപായിട്ട്, നിങ്ങൾക്ക് നമ്മുടെ കാര്യപരിപാടികൾ യൂട്യൂബിൽ ഇഷ്ടപ്പെടുന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ എന്തായാലും യൂട്യൂബിൽ ഒന്ന് സബ്സ്ക്രൈബ് ചെയ്തു കൂടെ കൂടുക. നമ്മളങ്ങനെ 9000 സബ്സ്ക്രൈബേഴ്സ് ആയിരിക്കുകയാണ്. ഇനി 10 കെ യിലേക്ക് അടുത്തോണ്ടിരിക്കുകയാണ്. സോ നിങ്ങൾ ഫോളോ ചെയ്യുകയാണ്, സബ്സ്ക്രൈബ് ചെയ്യുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ അത് പെട്ടെന്നാവും എന്ന് ഓർമ്മിപ്പിച്ചുകൊണ്ട്, വെൽക്കം ടു 80 പോഡ്കാസ്റ്റ് ഫുട്ബോൾ ക്ലബ്ബ് ആൻഡ് ദിസ് ഈസ് ആർ ജെ ആറ്റപ്പൻ. ആദ്യം തന്നെ പറയാനുള്ള ഒരു കാര്യം എന്ന് പറയുന്നത് 2010 ൽ സ്പെയിൻ വേൾഡ് കപ്പ് അടിക്കുന്ന ഒരു സമയമുണ്ട്. അതുകഴിഞ്ഞു കഴിഞ്ഞാൽ നേരെ അടുത്ത സീസൺ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിലേക്ക്, അതായത് ആ അടിച്ച വർഷത്തെ സീസൺ തുടങ്ങുന്നത് ഈ പറയുന്ന പോലെ തന്നെ ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയോടൊപ്പമാണ്. അതായത് 2010 മുതൽ 2013 വരെക്കുമാണ് ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോ ദി സ്പെഷ്യൽ വൺ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിൻ്റെ ഹെഡ് കോച്ച് ആയിട്ട് വന്നിട്ടുള്ളത്. ആൻഡ് ഇതിൻ്റെ ഇടയിൽ തന്നെ നമ്മൾ ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയെ കുറിച്ച് എപ്പോഴും പറയുമ്പോഴും ഈ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിൻ്റെ ഈയൊരു ചെറിയ സമയം എന്ന് വേണമെങ്കിൽ പറയാം, അല്ലെ? ഒരു മൂന്ന് വർഷം. അല്ലെങ്കിൽ നാല് വർഷം എന്ന്, നാല് വർഷം കൺസിഡർ ചെയ്യാൻ പറ്റില്ല പക്ഷേ എന്നാലും അങ്ങനെ. മൂന്ന് സീസൺസ്. ഈ മൂന്ന് സീസൺ കൊണ്ട് എങ്ങനെയാണ് റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിനെ ഈ പറയുന്ന പോലെ തന്നെ ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോ മാറ്റിയതെന്ന് വച്ച് കഴിഞ്ഞു കഴിഞ്ഞാൽ അത് ട്രോഫികളുടെ നമ്പർ വെച്ചിട്ടോ, വിന്നിങ് പെർസെൻ്റേജ് വെച്ചിട്ടോ, എൽ ക്ലാസിക്കോയിൽ അടിച്ചിട്ടുള്ള ജയങ്ങൾ വെച്ചിട്ടോ ഒന്നുമല്ല. പകരം ഹി വാസ് ബിൽഡിങ്. നമ്മുടെ ടോണി സ്റ്റാർക്ക് അയൺമാനിലൊക്കെ പറയുന്ന ഒരു സാധനമില്ലേ, ഐ ആം ദി മെക്കാനിക് എന്ന് പറയുന്ന പോലെ തന്നെ ഹി വാസ് ദി മാൻ ഹു ഡിസൈൻഡ് റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡ് എന്ന് വേണമെങ്കിൽ പറയാം. അതായത് രമണാ, എങ്ങനെയാ പറയാന്ന് വച്ചുകഴിഞ്ഞാൽ ആ ഒരു മൂന്ന് സീസൺ കൊണ്ട് റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിനെ ശരിയായ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡ് ആയിട്ട് മാറ്റാൻ ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയ്ക്ക് സാധിച്ചു എന്നുള്ളതാണ് ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയെ സംബന്ധിച്ചിടത്തോളവും റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിനെ സംബന്ധിച്ചിടത്തോളവും ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയുടെ സമയം പുള്ളിയുടെ പേര് വെച്ചുതന്നെ നമ്മൾ പറയുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ ഒരു സ്പെഷ്യൽ വൺ അല്ലെങ്കിൽ ഒരു സ്പെഷ്യൽ സീസൺ ആയി മാറുന്നത് എന്നുള്ളതാണ്. അത് എന്തുകൊണ്ടാണ് എന്ന് ചോദിക്കുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ, ഞാൻ ആ പറഞ്ഞ സമയം കൊണ്ട് തന്നെ പറഞ്ഞു വരികയാണ്. സ്പെയിൻ വേൾഡ് കപ്പ് അടിച്ചു കഴിഞ്ഞു കഴിഞ്ഞിട്ട് ബാഴ്സലോണയുടെ കാര്യമെടുത്ത് നോക്കുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ പിന്നെ അങ്ങോട്ട് ബാഴ്സലോണ യൂറോപ്പ് ഭരിച്ചിരുന്ന സമയമാണ്. എന്ന്
